analysis.one_liner: Permanently repeals the federal estate tax and generation-skipping transfer tax, ending them ahead of schedule.
analysis.headline: S. 13 would have permanently ended the estate tax starting January 1, 2005; introduced with 17 cosponsors, it was placed on the Senate calendar but never received a vote before the 108th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2001 tax law had already scheduled the estate tax and the generation-skipping transfer tax to disappear for a single year in 2010 and then come back. This bill would have made that repeal permanent and moved it up to the start of 2005. It was placed on the Senate calendar two weeks after introduction but was never called up for a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to the largest estates. Under the phase-in schedule in the 2001 law, the estate tax reached only estates above roughly $1.5 million per person by 2005, so the savings would flow almost entirely to the wealthiest few percent of families. The bill's title points to family farms and small businesses, but only a small share of those estates ever owed the tax at all; the repeal was also permanent, so no estate would face the tax's scheduled return in 2011.

how_it_helps.text: Permanently repeals the estate tax and the generation-skipping transfer tax, moving the 2001 law's one-year repeal forward from 2010 to January 1, 2005.
Removes the 2001 law's 2010 sunset for the estate tax repeal, so the tax never comes back after its temporary disappearance.

As the bill's stated purpose puts it, aims to give family farm and small business owners 'financial security... by ending the unfair practice of taxing someone at death' — the estates that do owe the tax would keep the business intact instead of selling assets to pay it.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury, which would permanently lose the revenue the estate tax raises from the largest estates. That money would have to be made up through higher taxes on everyone else, lower government spending, or more borrowing — a burden spread across households that never pay estate tax.

drawbacks.text: The repeal has no offset: the federal government permanently loses the estate tax's revenue, adding to deficits or forcing other taxes up or spending down. It would also have taken effect two years sooner than the 2001 law's schedule, deepening near-term budget gaps.

Because the tax applied only to estates above the exemption — about $1.5 million per person by 2005 under the phase-in — nearly all of the benefit goes to heirs of the wealthiest estates, while most family farms and small businesses never owed the tax at all.
It removes a tax that fell exclusively on very large inheritances, shifting more of the overall tax load onto wages and consumption, which ordinary households pay.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real but narrow: a permanent, accelerated tax cut concentrated on heirs of multimillion-dollar estates, enacted with no offset and no companion spending or tax changes. Weighed against the lost revenue and the added strain on everyone else's taxes or government services, the costs outweigh the benefits for most households.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, placed on the Senate calendar, and never brought up for a vote before the 108th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Jon Kyl introduced the bill on February 14, 2003; ten days later it was read a second time and placed on the Senate calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 20).
Nothing followed: no committee consideration, floor debate, or vote appears in the record for the rest of the Congress, and the bill died when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.
Under the 2001 tax law the estate tax was already scheduled to disappear in 2010 and return in 2011; this bill would have made the disappearance permanent and moved it up to 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal Treasury kept collecting estate tax from the largest estates through the 108th Congress, and taxpayers who would otherwise have covered the lost revenue are better off because the bill died. The estate tax's scheduled one-year repeal in 2010 still occurred under the 2001 law before Congress later reset the tax.

for.name: Sen. Jon Kyl
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make and accelerate permanent repeal of the estate and generation-skipping transfer taxes.

for.name: 17 senators (16 Republicans, 1 Democrat)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill shortly after introduction.

for.name: President George W. Bush
for.what_they_did: Publicly pressed Congress to make the 2001 estate tax repeal permanent as part of his 2003 tax agenda.

against.name: Bill Frist
against.what_they_did: Controlled the Senate floor agenda through the 108th Congress; S. 13 never received floor time or a vote after being placed on the calendar.

against.name: Senate Democratic minority
against.what_they_did: Opposed permanent estate tax repeal in this era and had blocked earlier repeal attempts with filibuster-sustaining votes, making floor time for repeal politically costly.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, so the chamber's split cannot be measured; of the 18 senators on the record for the bill (sponsor plus cosponsors), 17 were Republican and 1 was a Democrat.

industries.note: Repeal permanently spares estates above the exemption from the estate tax, so the savings concentrate in heirs of the largest fortunes. The offsetting revenue loss is spread across everyone else through deficits or other taxes.

industries.industry: Large family farms and closely held small businesses
industries.note: The bill's stated beneficiaries would keep more of the operation when an owner dies instead of selling assets to pay the tax. But only estates above the exemption ever paid the tax, so the real gain lands on the largest operations.

industries.industry: Estate-planning lawyers, wealth advisers, and life insurers
industries.note: The estate tax sustains a large industry of trust planning, valuation work, and tax-motivated insurance; repeal shrinks that fee base. Their preference for keeping the tax happens to align with preserving federal revenue.
